I have farmed these 9 mu in Quzhou for 45 years. I know every corner of this land, where it holds water and where it dries out first. It is early spring, my winter wheat is greening up, and I am already thinking through the whole year because every decision now locks in the harvest.

My wheat-maize rotation is the backbone of my household — I keep 6 mu in that double crop because wheat has a state floor price and maize feeds the livestock and sells to the grain traders. The remaining 3 mu I split between cotton and watermelon, 1.5 mu each, because cotton suits our local soil and watermelon brings good cash at the county summer market if the sweetness is right. My well gives me water when the rains fail, which they often do in May and early June.

Right now I am walking the wheat field and topdressing urea at the green-up stage. For that wheat I will use about 15 kg of nitrogen per mu across the season, split between last autumn’s basal dressing and this spring topdressing. I will irrigate four times total — the storage water I put down before winter, then jointing, heading, and grain filling. I spray twice: a herbicide early and one insecticide if aphids show up. I rotary till the wheat ground after the maize comes off in autumn. I expect 450 kg per mu if late spring does not turn too dry.

When the wheat comes off in early June, I waste no time. I plant hybrid maize seed the same day or the next, with no deep tillage — the soil is soft from the wheat roots and the summer heat is coming fast. I side-dress nitrogen at the big trumpet stage, about 16 kg per mu for the season, with modest phosphorus and potassium. I irrigate twice over the summer if the July rains are thin. Two sprays: a herbicide at emergence and insecticide if armyworm moths have been thick. I count on 550 kg per mu.

For cotton, I plough that 1.5 mu plot deep as soon as the ground thaws because cotton roots like a warm, loose seedbed. I plant improved seed in late April. Cotton is hungry for potassium, so I give it extra potash for the bolls. I irrigate three times — seedling establishment, flowering, and peak boll setting — and spray four times for bollworm, aphids, and red spider mites. I expect around 280 kg of seed cotton per mu.

The last 1.5 mu goes to watermelon. I rotary till it, shape the beds, and lay plastic mulch like the extension people taught us years ago. I plant hybrid seedlings in mid-April. Watermelon needs water control: I irrigate about eight times through the season, especially at fruit expansion, but I stop ten days before harvest so the sugar concentrates. It needs heavy potassium — 12 kg per mu — or the flesh turns watery and pale. I spray four times against wilt and melon fly. If prices hold, 2,500 kg per mu is a fair target.

At 60 years old, I do not chase every new technique, but I do use improved and hybrid seeds because they have proven themselves on my farm. I save my labor where I can — no deep ploughing for maize or watermelon — but I still turn the cotton ground by hand and plough because that crop rewards the effort.
